title: Strong resolution for pairs with small singular locus
statement:
Let $\mathscr P$ have objects pairs $(X,D)$ with $X$ a reduced Noetherian quasi-excellent scheme over $\mathbf Q$ [def-pc-reduced-scheme, pqf-def-locnoeth, def-exc-excellent-ring]. Noetherian means that $X$ has a finite affine cover by spectra of Noetherian rings; quasi-excellent means that the affine coordinate rings are quasi-excellent. The closed subscheme $D\subset X$ is an effective Cartier divisor, meaning its ideal is locally generated by one non-zero-divisor. Its underlying set contains every point where the local ring of $X$ is not regular [def-weil-regular-scheme]. As an abstract scheme, $D$ is a finite disjoint union of schemes of finite type over fields of characteristic zero [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]; different components may have different fields. Morphisms $(Y,E)\to(X,D)$ are regular morphisms $f:Y\to X$ with $E=Y\times_XD$, where regular means flat [def-weil-flat-morphism] with geometrically regular fibres: for every point $x\in X$ and every finite extension $k'$ of its residue field $\kappa(x)$, the base change $Y_x\times_{\kappa(x)}\operatorname{Spec}k'$ of the fibre [def-pc-scheme-fibre] is a regular scheme (in characteristic zero this is equivalent to regularity of $Y_x$). Include finite disjoint unions and the empty pair in $\mathscr P$.

There exists a single rule $H$ on $\mathscr P$ assigning to each pair a finite tower of ordinary blowups of $X$ [def-nagata-global-blowup], with coherent ideal centers [pqf-def-coherent], regular terminal scheme and nonempty regular nowhere dense centers. Every center lies over the singular locus of $X$. For every morphism of $\mathscr P$, $H(Y,E)$ is the scheme-theoretic pullback of $H(X,D)$ with exactly the empty centers removed, with all other extended ideal sheaves retained in their order. The empty pair has length zero. No independence of $H(X,D)$ from the auxiliary divisor $D$ is asserted.

source.place: Theorem 3.4.1 and category in §3.4.2, printed pp.25--26; existence of the strong variety input in §§1.3.1--1.3.2 and §2.3.5, as also recalled in ILO VIII Remark 2.3.11; Temkin, arXiv:0904.1592v2, read online 2026-10-24; archival copy WANTED. No Stacks tag states this desingularization result. ILO VIII 2.3.9--2.3.11 identifies this as the input for its Theorem 2.3.10.

proof.text: For $(X,D)$ put $I=\mathcal I_D$ and $(\mathfrak X,\mathfrak I)=(\widehat X_D,I\mathcal O_{\mathfrak X})$. By [lem-per-small-divisor-formal-completion] this is a reduced Noetherian quasi-excellent rig-regular locally principal formal scheme, a finite disjoint union of formal varieties in characteristic zero. All hypotheses hold: $I$ is Cartier, $X_{\mathrm{sing}}\subseteq|D|$, and the given components of $D$ are finite type over characteristic-zero fields. Choose once the single formal rule $\widehat F$ of [lem-per-rig-regular-formal-resolution] on the entire formal category, and let $T(X,D)=\widehat F(\mathfrak X,\mathfrak I)$. It is a finite centered formal tower; every center ideal is open and every center is nonempty and regular, lies over $\mathfrak X_{\mathrm{sing}}$, and the last formal level is regular.

source.place: Theorem 3.4.1, proof, first two sentences; Theorem 3.1.5

proof.text: Apply [lem-per-supported-formal-blowup-algebraization] to $Z=D$ and $T(X,D)$. Its open ideals make the tower $D$-supported. This gives a unique ordered ordinary tower, which defines $H(X,D)$, with coherent center ideals and the specified completion. The same correspondence identifies its centers with the formal centers, hence they are nonempty and regular. Since $X_{\mathrm{sing}}\subseteq |D|$, its regularity and singular-support clause gives a regular terminal scheme and centers over $X_{\mathrm{sing}}$; its reduced-input clause gives nowhere density. Thus this is a rule on all pairs, rather than separate choices of resolutions of individual schemes. For the empty pair the formal rule gives the empty tower and the correspondence gives length zero.

Let $f:(Y,E)\to(X,D)$ be a morphism of the given category. Since $E=Y\times_XD$, its ideal is $I\mathcal O_Y$. By [lem-per-regular-morphism-formal-completion] the induced map $\widehat f:\widehat Y_E\to\widehat X_D$ is regular. It respects the distinguished ideals: their extensions agree because both come from $I$. Consequently [lem-per-rig-regular-formal-resolution] identifies $T(Y,E)$ with the pullback of $T(X,D)$ after deletion of exactly the empty formal centers, retaining the other extended ideals in order. This uses regularity, not merely smoothness or a morphism over a common coefficient field.

The scheme morphism $f$ is flat. Form the cartesian pullback of $H(X,D)$ to $Y$. At every level the projection to the corresponding $X$-level is flat by [lem-weil-pbc-flat-morphism-base-change], so [thm-nagata-blowup-flat-base-change] identifies the next level with the ordinary blowup of the extended ideal. Complete this tower along the inverse images of $E$. By [lem-per-supported-formal-blowup-algebraization] its levels and centers complete to the formal blowup tower. The induced maps on its centers are the same as formal pullback: locally a supported center is defined modulo $I^N$, and both ordinary and completed pullback extend this same quotient ideal modulo $(I\mathcal O_Y)^N$. Therefore this completion is the uncontracted formal pullback used in Step 3.

By [lem-per-supported-formal-blowup-algebraization] a supported ordinary center is empty precisely when its formal center is empty, since they are the same closed scheme. Its ideal is then unit, and its blowup is an isomorphism by [cor-nagata-blowup-cartier-iso], applied to the invertible unit ideal. Delete exactly those stages from the ordinary pullback. Its completion is $T(Y,E)$ by Steps 3--4. Uniqueness in [lem-per-supported-formal-blowup-algebraization], now over $Y$ with $Z=E$, identifies it with $H(Y,E)$ including all retained ideals in their original order. Thus even a nonempty center inducing an isomorphism is retained. The construction depends on the completion with its distinguished ideal, so it asserts no independence from $D$.
